title: Implement a simple round-robin load balancer in Java (`AtomicInteger`).
shortTitle: Implement a simple round-robin load balancer in Java using AtomicInteger

s1_definition.profdef: A round-robin load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across a list of backend servers by cycling through them in order, server 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, and so on. In Java the thread-safe way to pick the next index without locks is an `AtomicInteger` whose `getAndIncrement` is atomically mapped onto the server list with a modulo, so concurrent threads each get a distinct, monotonically advancing counter value and no two threads collide on the same tick. For a production-grade balancer you also guard against unbounded counter growth, skip unhealthy nodes, and optionally weight servers by capacity.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has five teller counters serving customers like Rajesh and Priya. A round-robin host at the door sends the first customer to counter 1, the next to counter 2, and so on, looping back to counter 1 after counter 5, so every counter gets a fair, equal share and none is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The host keeps a single tally counter, and because many customers arrive at once, the tally must be updated atomically so two customers are never sent to the same counter by mistake and the count never gets corrupted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Round-robin cycles backends in order; an AtomicInteger's getAndIncrement modulo the server count gives a lock-free, thread-safe next pick.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A round-robin load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across a list of backend servers by cycling through them in order, server 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, and so on. In Java the thread-safe way to pick the next index without locks is an `AtomicInteger` whose `getAndIncrement` is atomically mapped onto the server list with a modulo, so concurrent threads each get a distinct, monotonically advancing counter value and no two threads collide on the same tick. For a production-grade balancer you also guard against unbounded counter growth, skip unhealthy nodes, and optionally weight servers by capacity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has five teller counters serving customers like Rajesh and Priya. A round-robin host at the door sends the first customer to counter 1, the next to counter 2, and so on, looping back to counter 1 after counter 5, so every counter gets a fair, equal share and none is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The host keeps a single tally counter, and because many customers arrive at once, the tally must be updated atomically so two customers are never sent to the same counter by mistake and the count never gets corrupted.

**One line to remember:** Round-robin cycles backends in order; an AtomicInteger's getAndIncrement modulo the server count gives a lock-free, thread-safe next pick.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea. Given a list of N backends, request number k goes to backend `k % N`. The only shared state is the counter k. If you used a plain `int` and did `index = counter++`, that is not thread-safe: under concurrency two threads can read the same value before either writes back, so they both pick the same backend and the distribution skews. You need the increment to be atomic.

Why AtomicInteger. `AtomicInteger.getAndIncrement()` performs a read-modify-write as one indivisible hardware-level compare-and-swap operation, so every concurrent caller receives a distinct value and the counter advances exactly once per call. You then map that value onto the list with modulo: `int index = Math.floorMod(counter.getAndIncrement(), servers.size())`. floorMod is used instead of the plain `%` operator because when the int counter eventually overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE it wraps to a negative number, and `%` would then produce a negative index that throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, whereas floorMod always returns a non-negative result in the range 0 to N-1.

Handling counter overflow. Over billions of requests the AtomicInteger will overflow. Using floorMod keeps the index valid even after the wrap, so correctness is preserved. Alternatively you can periodically reset or mask the counter, but floorMod is the simplest correct approach and is what I prefer.

Health checks and skipping dead nodes. A naive round-robin keeps sending traffic to a server that is down. A real balancer tracks each backend's health and, when it lands on an unhealthy one, advances to the next healthy one. You maintain a health flag per backend, updated by a background health-check pinger, and the pick loop skips unhealthy nodes, falling back gracefully if all are down.

Weighted round-robin. Not all servers are equal; a bigger instance can take more traffic. Weighted round-robin assigns each backend a weight and distributes proportionally, for example a weight-3 server gets three times the traffic of a weight-1 server. A simple implementation expands the list so a weight-3 server appears three times, or uses a smooth weighted algorithm that interleaves them to avoid bursts to one node.

Why this matters versus alternatives. Round-robin is stateless per request and gives even distribution when requests are roughly equal in cost, which is its strength and its weakness: if one request is very expensive it still counts as one tick, so round-robin does not account for actual load. Least-connections or least-response-time strategies adapt to real load but need more shared state. Round-robin's simplicity and the lock-free AtomicInteger make it extremely fast and contention-light, which is why it is a common default.

The senior nuance is contention. Under very high throughput even a single AtomicInteger can become a contention hotspot because every thread hits the same cache line. For extreme scale you can shard the counter or use a `LongAdder`-style striped counter, trading perfect ordering for throughput, since round-robin does not actually require globally perfect ordering, only roughly even distribution. For the vast majority of services a single AtomicInteger is more than fast enough.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's transfer API runs on multiple backend instances. A client-side load balancer in the gateway spreads incoming transfer requests across those instances.

Problem 1 — traffic was skewed to one instance. The first version used a plain int counter incremented without synchronization, so under load several threads read the same counter value and routed to the same backend, overloading it while others idled. This is why the next-index pick must use an AtomicInteger so every concurrent request gets a distinct tick.

Problem 2 — requests were sent to a crashed instance. When one backend died, round-robin kept sending every third request to it, and those requests failed. This is why the balancer must track health and skip unhealthy backends.

Problem 3 — a larger instance was underused. One backend had double the CPU but got the same share as the small ones. This is why we support weighted round-robin so the big instance takes proportionally more traffic.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo: a `Backend` with an address and health flag, a `RoundRobinLoadBalancer` using an AtomicInteger with floorMod that skips unhealthy nodes, and a `WeightedRoundRobinLoadBalancer`. It routes a burst of concurrent transfer requests for Rajesh and Priya, shows even distribution, shows skipping a downed node, and shows weighting.

```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/gateway-loadbalancer-1.0.0.jar com.bank.lb.LoadBalancerDemo

# Run as a gateway service
java -jar target/gateway-loadbalancer-1.0.0.jar

# Fire concurrent transfer requests through the balancer
for i in $(seq 1 9); do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}' &
done
wait
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three backends svc-1 (weight 1), svc-2 (weight 1), svc-3 (weight 2), and bursts of concurrent requests.

Step 1: Nine requests fire concurrently and each calls next. Each thread calls counter.getAndIncrement, which atomically hands out distinct values 0 through 8. No two threads get the same value, so no two collide on the same backend by accident.

Step 2: Each value is mapped with floorMod over size 3, producing indices 0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2. Over nine requests each of the three backends is picked exactly three times, an even distribution.

Step 3: svc-2 is marked unhealthy. Now six requests come in. Each call lands on an index via getAndIncrement; when it lands on svc-2 the health check fails, so the loop advances to the next index and returns a healthy backend. svc-2 receives zero requests; svc-1 and svc-3 share them.

Step 4: For weighted round-robin, the expanded list is [svc-1, svc-2, svc-3, svc-3] because svc-3 has weight 2 and appears twice. Eight requests cycle over this length-4 list twice, so svc-1 gets 2, svc-2 gets 2, and svc-3 gets 4, exactly double the others.

Step 5: Over billions of requests the AtomicInteger would overflow past Integer.MAX_VALUE into negatives, but floorMod still returns a valid non-negative index, so routing stays correct forever.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Even distribution over 9 requests: {transfer-svc-1:8080=3, transfer-svc-2:8080=3, transfer-svc-3:8080=3}
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] After svc-2 down (skipped): {transfer-svc-1:8080=3, transfer-svc-3:8080=3}
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Weighted over 8 requests (svc-3 weight=2): {transfer-svc-1:8080=2, transfer-svc-2:8080=2, transfer-svc-3:8080=4}
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
A round-robin load balancer distributes requests evenly across a list of backends by cycling through them in order, so request k goes to backend k modulo N. The only shared state is the counter, and that is exactly where thread safety matters. If I use a plain int and do index equals counter plus plus, that is not atomic: under concurrency two threads can read the same value before either writes it back, so they route to the same backend and the distribution skews, which is a bug we actually hit when one instance got overloaded while others sat idle. The fix is an AtomicInteger, whose getAndIncrement is a single indivisible compare-and-swap, so every concurrent caller receives a distinct, monotonically advancing value and no two collide.

I map that counter onto the backend list with Math.floorMod rather than the plain percent operator. This is a detail I always mention: over billions of requests the int counter overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE and wraps to a negative number, and the percent operator would then produce a negative index that throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, whereas floorMod always returns a non-negative result in the valid range, so routing stays correct forever even after the overflow. This gives a completely lock-free next-pick that is extremely fast and contention-light.

A production balancer does more than cycle blindly. It tracks each backend's health with a flag updated by a background health-check pinger, and when the pick lands on an unhealthy node it advances to the next healthy one, which is how I fixed requests being sent to a crashed instance. It also supports weighted round-robin for unequal instances: a bigger server gets a larger weight and proportionally more traffic, which I implement simply by expanding the list so a weight-two server appears twice and then round-robining over the expanded list with the same AtomicInteger trick. Over eight requests, a weight-two backend among three then receives four while the others receive two each.

I am also aware of the trade-offs. Round-robin treats every request as one equal tick, so it does not account for a single very expensive request, which is where least-connections or least-response-time strategies adapt better at the cost of more shared state. And at extreme throughput even one AtomicInteger can become a cache-line contention hotspot, in which case I would shard the counter or use a striped counter, because round-robin only needs roughly even distribution, not globally perfect ordering. For the vast majority of services a single AtomicInteger with floorMod and health-aware skipping is more than fast enough.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I implement round-robin with an AtomicInteger whose getAndIncrement gives each concurrent request a distinct tick, I map it to a backend with floorMod so overflow never breaks the index, and I extend it with health-aware skipping and weighted expansion so the balancer is thread-safe, lock-free, resilient to dead nodes, and fair to unequal instances.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
